title: HTTP and HTTPS: the language of web requests
dek: Nearly every call the Zotato apps make is an HTTP request: a method, a path, some headers and maybe a body, answered by a status, headers and a body. Knowing which methods are safe to repeat, what status codes mean, and what HTTPS does and doesn't protect covers most of what an interview will ask about it.

items: HTTP is request and response: the client sends a method and a path with headers and an optional body; the server answers with a status code, headers and a body.
Each request stands alone (HTTP is stateless), which is what lets any server behind a load balancer answer it. Keep state in databases and caches, not in the server's memory.
HTTPS encrypts the request on the way. It does not make the request trustworthy: always check who is asking from the token, never from values the client sent.

body.x: HTTP/1.1 is plain text, so you can read it. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send the same information in binary frames, but the parts are the same.

body.cap: A request names a method and a path and adds headers; a response gives a status, headers and a body. Here the client offered gzip or br compression and the server picked br, so the 18 KB menu travelled as about 4 KB.

body.x: The headers carry a lot of quiet negotiation. `Accept-Encoding` says which compressions the client can undo, and `Content-Encoding` says which one the server used. `Accept` and `Content-Type` do the same for formats, `Accept-Language` for languages, and `Cache-Control` tells browsers and CDNs how long a response may be reused. It is a good pattern for your own APIs too: let the client say what it can handle, and let the server choose.

body.x: 'Safe to repeat' (idempotent) matters more than it looks. Networks fail between the request and the response, and clients, proxies and load balancers retry. A repeated GET or PUT is harmless; a repeated POST can create a second order or a second charge. The article on failing calls in this tab shows how idempotency keys make a POST safe to retry.

body.x: The first digit is what clients act on: 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx the client must change something (retrying the same request won't help), 5xx the server failed (a retry, later, might work). Getting 4xx and 5xx right is what lets retry logic behave.

Each HTTP request carries everything needed to answer it: the path, the parameters and a token that says who is asking. The server keeps nothing about the client between requests. That is what lets Zotato run thirty identical API servers behind a load balancer and send each request to any of them, and lets a server be replaced in the middle of the day without anyone noticing. A useful way to think of a simple API server is as a function from the request (plus the database) to a response.
HTTPS: what it protects, and what it doesn't

HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. TLS encrypts everything after the handshake, so nobody on the network (the café's Wi-Fi, an internet provider) can read or change the request, and the certificate proves the phone is talking to the real api.zotato.in. Every public site and API should use it; browsers warn on anything else.

body.cap: TLS protects the request between the app and the server. It doesn't protect the server from the app: anyone can edit their own requests, so the server checks every id against the user in the signed token.

body.x: The mistake to avoid is trusting what the client sends because the connection is secure. A user can change any part of their own request: an order id in the path, a price in the body, a userId field. The server must take the user's identity from a signed token or session and check that this user may read or change this order. Sending ids in the body is fine; believing them is not.

items: Use the right method and a sensible status for each endpoint, and say which writes are safe to retry.
Mention HTTPS once for anything public, then move on. Say how the server knows who the caller is (a token checked on every request).
Say that API servers are stateless and why: any server can answer, so you can add and replace them freely.

body.label: Go deeper: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

body.x: HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers open up to six connections per site to load a page in parallel. HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over one connection as separate streams and compresses headers, which helps mobile apps that make many small calls.

Because HTTP/2 still runs on TCP, one lost packet stalls every stream until it is resent. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, where each stream is ordered separately, so a loss only delays its own stream; it also sets up faster. Servers usually offer all three, and clients use the newest they support.
